funFacts: groß is the same word as English great and Dutch groot.
groß- in family words works like English grand-: Großvater, Großmutter, Großeltern (S06).
Swiss Standard German writes no ß: gross, grösser.
pitfalls: Tall of a person is groß (Er ist groß), not hoch – hoch is for buildings, mountains and trees (ein hohes Haus).
The comparative has an umlaut: größer, am größten (not *großer, *am großten).
subtleties: mein großer Bruder / meine große Schwester = my older brother / sister, not necessarily taller.
Height is said with groß: Ich bin 1,70 (Meter) groß.
Before a noun it takes an ending (ein großes Haus, der große Tisch); after sein it takes none (Das Haus ist groß).

etymology.text: From Middle High German hōch, from Old High German hōh, from Proto-West Germanic *hauh, from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kewk-. Compare Dutch hoog, English high, Swedish hög. The declension from the stem hoh- goes back to Old High German -h-, which became /x/ at the end of a syllable but stayed /h/ (later silent) elsewhere; standard German kept this alternation only in hoch.

funFacts: hoch, Dutch hoog and English high are the same Germanic word.
Hochdeutsch (High German) was first named after the higher, southern part of the German-speaking lands, not after being “better” German.

Comparison: höher, am höchsten – umlaut, and the c comes back in the superlative.
subtleties: People are groß, never hoch; a building can be both: ein hohes Haus (tall) / ein großes Haus (big, roomy).

subtleties: Comparison: schlechter, am schlechtesten (der schlechteste …).

subtleties: One word for things and people, where Greek says παλιός (things) and ηλικιωμένος / γέρος (people), and English adds elderly.
